analysis.one_liner: Ends the program letting colleges act as federally subsidized student loan lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop colleges from lending federal student loan money to their own students died in committee with 0 cosponsors and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the "school as lender" program, under which colleges could make federal student loans directly and collect federal subsidy payments on them. It would also cancel a 2005 provision that had opened lender status to for-profit colleges, and apply to loans first paid out on or after July 1, 2007. The bill was referred to the Senate education committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and families, who would borrow under a system where their own school is not also the lender collecting federal subsidies on their debt. Taxpayers would also save the federal payments that go to schools acting as lenders, since the program pays lenders a government subsidy on every loan.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the provisions of the Higher Education Act that let colleges serve as eligible lenders in the federal guaranteed loan program, ending the arrangement in which a school makes loans to its own students and receives federal subsidy payments on them.

It repeals Section 8011 of the 2005 Higher Education Reconciliation Act, which had newly allowed for-profit colleges to become eligible lenders, closing a channel through which for-profit schools could profit from their own students' federal debt.
The repeal takes effect for loans first disbursed on or after July 1, 2007, so new student borrowing would no longer flow through schools acting as lenders.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges, including for-profit schools, that were acting as lenders or had newly gained the right to would lose the federal subsidy revenue they collected on loans. Private banks and loan companies that dominate the federal guaranteed loan program would pick up the lending volume instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Colleges acting as student loan lenders

drawbacks.text: Schools acting as lenders collected federal subsidy payments, and some used that revenue to help fund their aid operations; repealing the program takes that money away from those schools.
The bill was a one-page, single-sponsor measure that never received a hearing or committee analysis, so its effects on schools and on the loan market were never examined on the record.
It is narrow: it removes schools as lenders but leaves the rest of the federally subsidized private-lender loan system, with its other lender subsidies, untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it closes a specific conflict of interest in which a student's school was also the subsidized lender profiting on the student's debt. The cost falls on a small set of schools that collected the subsidy payments, some of which put that money back into aid. Because the bill never got a hearing, no one weighed those trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: Schumer introduced it with only days left in the 2006 session; it went to the Senate education committee and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on September 29, 2006, near the end of the 109th Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No senator joined as a cosponsor, and the committee never reported the bill or scheduled it for action before the Congress expired on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The schools and for-profit colleges that were lending federal loan money to their own students, and collecting federal subsidy payments for it, kept that arrangement for another Congress. The private lenders who dominate the guaranteed loan program also kept the lending volume to themselves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schools and lenders profiting from school-as-lender

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the school as lender program; it was his only action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; the bill died in committee with no hearing or vote.

against.name: Michael Enzi
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the final months of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors on either side, so no partisan split shows up in the record; the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The 2005 reconciliation law had just opened federal lender status to for-profit institutions, and this bill repeals that provision. For-profit schools were the heaviest users of school-as-lender arrangements, which let them earn federal subsidies on loans to their own students.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities acting as FFEL lenders
industries.note: These schools lose the federal subsidy payments they collected as lenders, revenue that some recycled into aid operations. The bill's premise is that a school profiting on its own students' debt is a conflict of interest.

industries.industry: Private student loan companies and banks in the FFEL program
industries.note: With schools barred from lending, the guaranteed-loan volume stays with the private lenders the program was built around. Borrowers would still get federal loans; the banks' gain is mainly the loss of a competitor, not money out of students' pockets.
